title: The Weight of Gold
summary: In the mountain mine above Coldhollow, the gold weighs according to the greed of whoever takes it — a little for the needy, a crushing burden for the grasping. When Doran's village falls on hard times, he goes down for just enough, and learns that the mine measures not how much you take, but why.

chapters.title: The Mine That Weighed the Heart
chapters.body:
Above the village of Coldhollow, high in the grey mountain, there was a mine full of gold — and everyone knew about it, and almost no one dared take from it, because of the mountain's strange and ancient law.

The gold in the mountain weighed according to the heart of whoever took it. That was the law, old as the peak itself. A person who took gold out of true need — to feed a hungry family, to help a struggling neighbor, to meet a real and honest want — would find the gold light as feathers in their hands, easy to carry down, a gift freely given by the mountain. But a person who took gold out of greed — who took more than they needed, who took to hoard, to grow rich, to have for the sake of having — would find that same gold growing heavier and heavier the more they grasped, until the weight of it crushed them, pinned them, buried them in the very tunnels they'd hoped to plunder. The mountain did not measure how much you took. It measured why. And it was never, ever wrong.

The folk of Coldhollow told the story to their children as both a promise and a warning. Over the generations, a few desperate, honest souls had gone up in times of true hardship and come down with a little light gold, exactly enough, and been saved by it. And a few greedy souls had gone up dreaming of riches — and never come down at all, crushed somewhere in the dark under the impossible weight of their own grasping. The mountain gave freely to the needy and buried the greedy, and so the mine sat mostly untouched, a test that most people were wise enough never to take.

Doran was fourteen, and the winter had been cruel to Coldhollow.

A failed harvest and a hard frost had left the whole village hungry and cold, and Doran's own family — his little sisters, his ailing mother — were among the worst off, with almost nothing left in the larder and a long cold month still ahead before spring. Doran was the eldest, and he felt the weight of his family's need like a stone in his own chest, and he lay awake at night trying to think how to keep his sisters fed.

And he thought of the mine.

He knew the law. He knew the danger. He knew that people who went up the mountain grasping never came down. But he also knew that the gold was light for those who took from true need — and if ever there was true need, it was now, with his sisters hungry and his mother ill and the larder nearly bare. He didn't want to be rich. He just wanted to keep his family alive through the winter. Surely, he thought, that was exactly the kind of need the mountain gave to freely.

So Doran resolved to go up the mountain, into the mine, and take gold — just enough, only enough, to see his family and perhaps his neighbors through to spring. And he told himself, firmly, as he climbed the grey slope in the cold dawn, that he would take only what he needed, and not one flake more, because he had heard all his life what the mountain did to those who grasped.

chapters.title: Just Enough
chapters.body:
The mine was dark and cold and old, and Doran went down into it with a single candle, his heart pounding, and soon he found the gold.

It was everywhere — veins of it running through the black rock, nuggets of it glinting in the walls, more wealth than Coldhollow had seen in a hundred years, all just sitting there in the dark waiting to be taken. And Doran felt, at once, the pull of it. The greed the mountain warned of was not some obvious wickedness that only bad people felt. It was a quiet, reasonable-sounding voice, and it spoke to Doran the moment he saw all that gold. Take a little extra, it whispered. Just a little more than you need, to be safe. What if spring comes late? What if next winter is hard too? Take extra, just in case. Take enough to never be hungry again. Who would blame you?

Doran reached out and took a single nugget of gold, meaning to test its weight, and it was light — light as a feather in his palm, easy and warm, the mountain giving freely. Because in that moment his heart was true: he was thinking of his hungry sisters, and this one nugget was for them, and the mountain knew it. Emboldened, Doran gathered what he judged his family would truly need to get through the winter — enough for food, enough for warmth, enough to share a little with the neighbors who were suffering too. And all of it stayed light in his sack, feather-light, the mountain approving, because every bit of it was taken from real need with a true heart.

He had enough. He knew he had enough. He should have turned and climbed out then, with his light sack of exactly-enough gold, and been saved.

But the quiet voice whispered again, looking at all the gold still glittering in the walls. Just a little more. You're already here. You may never be able to come back. Think how safe you'd be — you and your sisters — if you took just a bit extra. Not out of greed. Out of caution. Out of love for them, even. Wouldn't a good brother make sure they were safe forever, not just through this one winter?

And Doran, who was a good boy, and who did love his sisters, listened to the voice — because it dressed itself up as love and caution and good sense, and did not look like greed at all. He began to gather more. More than his family needed. More than the neighbors needed. Gold for next winter, and the winter after, and to never be poor again, and to be safe, safe, safe forever.

And the gold in his sack began to grow heavy.

At first he barely noticed — a little drag on his shoulder. But as he kept gathering, kept listening to the voice that said just a little more, the weight grew, and grew, faster than the amount he added. The sack that had been feather-light when it held exactly enough was now pulling hard at him, then dragging, then so heavy he could barely lift it. And Doran understood, with a cold spike of fear, exactly what was happening. He had crossed the line. Somewhere between taking what he needed and taking to be safe forever, his true need had curdled into greed — the quiet, reasonable, love-disguised greed that the mountain weighed and judged. And the gold was growing heavier by the second, because he was still grasping, and the mountain was still measuring, and the weight of his grasping was about to bury him in the dark.

chapters.title: What He Chose to Carry
chapters.body:
The sack grew heavier and heavier, dragging Doran down, and the tunnel seemed to press in around him, and he understood that if he kept grasping — if he tried to carry all this gold he'd gathered out of fear and greed — the mountain would crush him under its weight, and he would never come down, and his sisters would starve waiting for a brother who never returned.

He fell to his knees under the crushing weight of the sack, and he saw, with terrible clarity, the whole shape of his mistake. He had come for true need, and the mountain had given freely. But he hadn't been able to stop at enough. The voice that said just a little more, that dressed greed up as love and caution, had led him past his real need into grasping — and grasping is grasping, however kindly it disguises itself, and the mountain was never fooled. He was being buried not because he'd taken gold, but because he'd taken more than he needed, out of a fear of not having enough, which is the truest root of greed there is.

And Doran understood what he had to do, and it was hard, because the quiet voice fought him even now. He had to let the extra go. All of it — everything he'd gathered beyond his true need, all the gold for next winter and the winter after and being safe forever. He had to set it down, here in the dark, and take only what he'd first gathered: exactly enough, and not one flake more.

It was harder than it should have been. The gold was so beautiful, and the fear was so real — what if spring came late, what if next winter was cruel, what if enough wasn't enough? The voice screamed at him to keep it, to find a way to carry it, to not be a fool and leave a fortune in the dark. But Doran had felt the weight of his own grasping, literally crushing him into the stone, and he knew the voice for what it was now. So he opened the sack, and he poured out all the extra — all the gold he'd taken out of greed and fear — and kept only what his family and neighbors truly needed to survive the winter.

And the moment he let the extra go, the sack grew light again.

Feather-light, warm, easy — exactly as it had been when he'd taken only what he needed. The crushing weight lifted. The tunnel seemed to open up around him. The mountain, which had been about to bury him, gave freely once more — because his heart was true again, emptied of grasping, holding only real need. Doran wept with relief in the dark, and shouldered his light sack of exactly-enough gold, and climbed up out of the mine into the cold bright dawn, saved.

He brought the gold down to Coldhollow, and it was exactly enough — enough to feed his family through the winter, and to share with the neighbors who were suffering, so that the whole village made it through to spring. Not a fortune. Not riches. Not safety forever. Just enough, honestly taken, freely given by a mountain that had measured his heart and, in the end, found it true.

And Doran never went back to the mine, though he could have, though the gold still glittered up there in the dark. Because he had learned the thing the mountain existed to teach, and he had learned it with the weight of it crushing him into the stone: that the danger was never in taking what you need. The danger was in the quiet voice that says just a little more — the voice that dresses greed up as love, and fear, and good sense, and leads you, flake by reasonable flake, from honest need into a grasping that will bury you. Enough, Doran understood now, is a kind of wisdom. Knowing when you have enough, and being able to stop, and letting the rest go — that is the thing that keeps the gold light in your hands and the mountain from closing over your head.

He grew up to be a man of modest means and great contentment, and when his own children asked him why he never went up to the mine that had made a few families rich and buried so many others, he told them the truth: "I went up once, and took exactly enough, after nearly taking far too much. And I learned that exactly enough, held with an open and grateful heart, weighs nothing at all — while just a little more, grasped out of fear, weighs enough to bury you. The mountain doesn't measure how much you carry. It measures why. And a heart that knows when to stop is the only thing that ever comes down that mountain alive."
